title: Inside the Regime-Adaptive Portfolio - Systematic Investor - Ep.377

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Inside the Regime-Adaptive Portfolio - Systematic Investor - Ep.377.docx

speakers: Alan Dunne (Archive Capital, co-host; transcript spelling Alan Don)
summary: Systematic Investor Ep. 377: trend following in a policy-shock year, 2025 performance and SocGen index changes, then Alan Dunne's paper on a regime-adaptive portfolio (40% growth, 40% adaptive, 20% diversifiers by risk). Conclusions: new macro regime (stickier inflation, high debt, positive stock-bond correlation) needs adaptive strategies; labels like alternative mislead.

coverage.note: Disclaimers and intro; Fed chair odds (Hassett) on prediction market
Fed chair independence; Vanguard crypto; MSTR index; question on political shocks
Trend in policy shocks: 2012, COVID; short-term trend; Liberation Day
Yen carry unwind; trend barometer; November performance
2025 index performance; SocGen index AUM cutoffs and changes
Index consolidation (constituent list skipped); Fed macro view; tariffs study start
Tariff study; bond yields and regime; 1990s parallel
AI productivity vs demand; debt levels; fiscal dominance question
Yield drivers; Marks and White quotes; paper motivation
Macro regime change; debt and equity valuation; problems with labels
Adaptive strategies; 40/40/20 risk portfolio; correlation regimes
Inflation uncertainty and trend; total portfolio approach
Reference portfolios; alternatives as growth; standalone optimisation
Morningstar labeling of return-stacked products; outro

completeness_estimate: 0.96 - first reader captured almost all claims with correct speakers and numbers; only the small-tariff caveat on the SF Fed study and the squandered-credibility point were missing

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: So clearly money talk. So the suspicion is somebody who has information um is betting on him becoming the next Fed chair.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne

claims.claim: A Hassett Fed chair would likely be more dovish, supporting the administration view of a productivity boom and disinflation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: can he truly be independent if he takes on the job of Fed chair.
claims.claim: Closeness of the likely Fed chair to the administration raises doubt about Fed independence.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we saw a change in the fundamentals at at at some point where we saw um weaker economic growth and a breakout in European bonds and a sell off in the euro and and a breakout in in oil prices.
claims.claim: The 2012 risk-on risk-off choppy period ended when fundamentals changed and breakouts appeared, as choppy phases for trend end eventually.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we had co which was kind of a new jolt for markets and knocked the economy out of secular stagnation and into a new regime.
claims.claim: Trend's tough late-2010s period eased from 2019, and COVID shifted the economy out of secular stagnation, restoring trend conditions.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: this year has turned out to be a pretty horrible year for short-term strategies.
claims.claim: Despite expectations that policy reversals would help short-term trend, short-term trend strategies had a very bad 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: most of the outperformance that they have seen in their strategy this year came around liberation day
claims.claim: Annual results can depend on a few events (e.g. Liberation Day gains for one manager), so investors should take a long-term view.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if we have a yen carry on wind I would expect it to be negative for for for trend followers in those markets.
claims.claim: Trend followers are short yen, especially on yen crosses; a yen carry unwind would hurt them, depending on speed and context.
claims.indicator: trend positioning in yen and yen crosses
claims.testable: yes - CFTC positioning and trend returns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I've heard this argument I mean so many times in the last two years and yet it continues to trend higher
claims.claim: Consensus bearish calls on Swiss franc/yen crosses have been wrong for two years as the trend persisted, showing that trends outlast commentary.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: most of the exposure is not necessarily in outright in the end but it might be in JGB's um at the moment.
claims.claim: Trend exposure to Japan may be more in JGBs than in outright yen.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer finished yesterday at 39 which is on the weaker side
claims.claim: Niels's trend barometer of 39 signals a neutral to slightly weak start to December.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it was like the fifth or sixth consecutive positive month maybe the fifth pos consecutive positive month.
claims.claim: Many trend managers had five or six consecutive positive months into November 2025, after a tough start to 2025.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the short-term traders index down eight basis points um so far, but down 5.41% uh in 2025
claims.claim: As of Dec 2025, trend indices were about flat to slightly negative for 2025 (SocGen CTA -1.6%, Trend +0.2%) and short-term traders -5.4%, while MSCI World was +20.7%, S&P 500 +17.8% and bonds +7.1%.
claims.indicator: SocGen CTA, Trend, short-term indices vs equities

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the cutoff level for 2026 looks like it's going to be around 1.9 billion in the program.
claims.claim: SocGen index AUM cutoffs for 2026: about $1.9B for the CTA index and $4.64B in one strategy for the Trend index, which favours large managers.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: now as far as I can tell their largest strategy is no more short-term it is actually their trend following program
claims.claim: Crabel's largest strategy is now its trend program, not short-term, suggesting long-term strategies are more viable than short-term.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: how we're seeing maybe the largest trend followers getting bigger and and just consolidating um their their position
claims.claim: The high AUM cutoff suggests the largest trend followers are consolidating their position in the index.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we're seeing the Fed cutting rates at a time when inflation has settled very much above target
claims.claim: The Fed is cutting while inflation sits above target and progress to 2% has stalled, with a split Fed.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: unemployment tends to to rise um straight away when tariffs come in.
claims.claim: A San Francisco Fed 40-year cross-country study found that tariffs raise unemployment immediately and lower inflation first, then raise inflation over the next two years.
claims.conditions: Historical tariff changes were smaller than now

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think from that perspective there is a little bit of of comp maybe complacency around the markets
claims.claim: Markets are complacent about Fed cuts with inflation above target and tariff pass-through still ahead.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the savings investment um relationship has shifted more towards you know stronger investment demand uh pushing up uh pressure on yields versus the old regime where we had excess supply pushing down yields.
claims.claim: Global yields are rising (JGB, German 25-year, no news) because stronger investment demand (AI data centers, defense) shifted the savings-investment balance from excess savings to scarcer capital; the US 10-year (4.1%) is the outlier.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: What was fueling productivity growth at the time was more use of personal computers.
claims.claim: In the 1990s productivity came from diffusion of earlier tech (PCs) while internet infrastructure gave demand, so the AI parallel is superficial.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: yes we're seeing the demand influence but bit early to say h we're seeing the the uh supply side benefits yet
claims.claim: AI spending adds to GDP arithmetically but evidence of productivity gains is mixed (McKinsey: more trying than use; St. Louis Fed: marginal gains).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the debt GDP level in the US is is double what it was uh in 1999.
claims.claim: US debt/GDP is double its 1999 level and the 1999 fiscal surplus is gone, so high equity valuations and high debt make the setting much more unstable than the 1990s.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: And in 2017, 20% um, responded yes, which actually to me that's is surprisingly large back then.
claims.claim: In the McKinsey survey AI use rose from 20% in 2017 to 88% today, showing adoption is widespread.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: why were bond yields going down all the time? Because of this excess savings from from Asia and then in the 2010s, bonds went negative.
claims.claim: Falling yields from Greenspan's conundrum through the 2010s reflected excess savings and capital-light tech; the AI capex boom, defence spending and no appetite for austerity reverse this.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It is that they conclude that the way things are today is the way it'll always be and the things that have been happening will continue to happen.
claims.claim: The biggest investor mistake is to assume current conditions persist (Howard Marks).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: systems always break down. The lesson is be prepared.
claims.claim: Financial systems always break down, so prepare (Bill White).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: all of these things were disinflationary forces um which led to to to lower inflation and more stable inflation
claims.claim: From the 1980s a 40-year disinflation (Volcker, China trade, Soviet collapse, free-market acceptance, central bank independence) created a great moderation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: inflation is going to be higher and stickier.
claims.claim: Since 2020 the regime is higher, stickier inflation with shocks (COVID, Ukraine) and a changed bond-equity correlation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: every time you've got a recession, you get a a step change higher.
claims.claim: US debt/GDP steps higher in each recession, so another recession would worsen fiscal sustainability.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: US households own about I think it's about $40 trillion of equities.
claims.claim: With households owning about $40T of equities, an equity bear market could wipe out $20T of wealth, so the economy is more levered to equities.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: that could be the the straw that breaks the the camel's back
claims.claim: High debt with high equity valuations is a combined risk that raises the probability of fiscal dominance and financial repression.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: greater risk of tail outcomes whether it's runaway inflation or or even you know a deleveraging disinflation or deflation.
claims.claim: Both runaway inflation and deflationary deleveraging are plausible tail outcomes, with the bond-equity correlation less stable and more positive.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it has a low correlation to equities when equities are going up but it doesn't have a low correlation it tends to be positively correlation when equities are going down
claims.claim: Credit looks diversifying in up markets but correlates positively in equity declines, so labels such as 'alternative' mislead.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: trend following can be proactive. It can be progrowth, pro- risk at times when when the equities are trending higher.
claims.claim: Trend is more like a midfielder than defence: it can be pro-growth when equities trend up and reduce risk when conditions change.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the framework has a 40% allocation of risk to growth 40% to adaptive strategies and 20% to diversifying assets and strategies
claims.claim: The proposed portfolio allocates risk 40% growth, 40% adaptive (trend, macro), 20% diversifiers, using return stacking and leverage and risk contribution rather than capital weights.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: rolling equity beta of a uh of this adaptive portfolio which swings much more dramatically uh from from kind of negative to over one than say a 60/40 portfolio
claims.claim: The adaptive portfolio's rolling equity beta swings from negative to above one, unlike the constant roughly 0.6 of 60/40.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: every time interest rates uh go above 3 4% uh the correlation tends to uh go positive.
claims.claim: Over 125 years, when interest rates exceed 3 to 4% the stock-bond correlation turns positive.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it could well be something that I think trend following tends to do better in those kind of environments um where inflation may not be high, but it's not stable at least.
claims.claim: Trend should do well when inflation is unstable even if not high.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: there's an an increased risk of of inflation expectations being deankered.
claims.claim: After the 2021-22 inflation spike, sensitivity is higher and the risk of de-anchored expectations is greater.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I do look at instances where inflation was uh 1 percentage point above its its two-year average and 1% below.
claims.claim: In the paper, trend following stands out when inflation surprises up or down by 1 percentage point versus its two-year average.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: is equivalent to kind of using a 6040 as a as a benchmark but with about an 8% tracking error
claims.claim: The adaptive portfolio has about 8% tracking error to 60/40, versus CalPERS about 4% to its 75/25, with more flexibility than a total portfolio approach.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: still start off with a with with with a um with a reference portfolio.
claims.claim: Total portfolio approaches still start from a reference portfolio embedded in old thinking, limiting flexibility.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you've got assets like private equity venture capital they're they're alternative growth
claims.claim: Private equity and venture capital are alternative growth assets, a private form of public equity risk, not diversifiers; the bar for diversifier is higher.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you are optimizing a hedge fund portfolio by itself on a standalone basis you get a different outcome
claims.claim: A JP Morgan AM / GIC study showed standalone hedge fund optimisation picks convergent strategies, while a total portfolio view picks pure diversifiers (macro, trend, commodities).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: don't forget Marovit's optimization was based on the idea of you find the best risk adjusted return. You blend based on the on the best asset allocation.
claims.claim: Markowitz logic: choose the best risk-adjusted blend first and then set risk with leverage or deleverage, not by shifting between equities and bonds.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: for a lot of people if you want more risk that naturally means more equities just to get the volatility up
claims.claim: Capital constraints cause underallocation to diversifiers; futures leverage removes this constraint.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: people often judge these strategies from the perspective of the last 15 years when we've had a you know a fantastic equity bull market
claims.claim: Judging diversifying strategies by the past 15-year equity bull market is misleading when equity returns are likely lower going forward.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you break it down into how much of the portfolio is linked to growth it could be 80%
claims.claim: A typical institutional portfolio with 10 to 12 buckets is 80% growth-linked, and over 90% in risk terms, so it is concentrated in growth and stable inflation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: as we saw in the 196682 period we had higher inflation but equities got derated amid much more macro volatility.
claims.claim: In 1966-82 high inflation derated equities, so equities are not a reliable inflation hedge.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when a you know a major economy like this US start behaving like an emerging market runaway inflation is the obvious risk
claims.claim: A major economy behaving like an emerging market risks runaway inflation, or after a boom and tightening, asset deleveraging deflation; portfolios are not prepared.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: 50 60% equities 20% fixed income some hedge funds but not enough small amount of gold.
claims.claim: Typical wealth portfolios are 50 to 60% equities, 20% fixed income and little gold or hedge funds, so they need rebalancing and leverage tools.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the benefit comes from the notably lower draw downs you you see in the portfolio because the adaptive strategies have that ability to respond during the major crisis
claims.claim: The adaptive portfolio beats 60/40 since 1990 mainly through smaller drawdowns, which compound from a higher base after recoveries.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the strategy doesn't outperform in every period or not even in every 5year period.
claims.claim: The portfolio does not outperform in every period; 2015-2019 was best for 60/40, so it is built for robustness over the next 10 years rather than any scenario.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the approach has done better historically even during that kind of disinflationary period
claims.claim: The approach did better even in the disinflationary period, making it a more robust method for the future.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the worst thing that can happen as you enter retirement is that you get a big um draw down in in your portfolio.
claims.claim: With many people near retirement, smoother returns matter because a big drawdown near retirement is worst.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: to think more in terms of risk terms, not just uh notional allocations
claims.claim: Think in risk terms, use futures, return stacking and portable alpha as building blocks, and combine adaptive strategies to overcome behavioural obstacles to holding them.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you put the word leverage into the um labeling, then that becomes a problem for many platforms to even carry those products on their uh on their platform.
claims.claim: Morningstar's new 'levered multiasset' category for return-stacked products could restrict platform distribution; Alan suggests 'unconstrained multiasset'.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: obviously the historic um changes in tariffs have been much smaller relative to
claims.claim: Caveat on the San Francisco Fed 40-year cross-country tariff study: historical tariff changes were much smaller than the 2025 US tariffs, so its unemployment-then-inflation pattern may understate or misstate today's effects.
claims.indicator: historical tariff changes vs 2025 tariff size
claims.conditions: out-of-sample tariff shock far larger than history
claims.testable: partly - check dose-response of tariff size in the panel

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the inflation fighting credibility has been squandered somewhat. I mean it was it was hard one you know Vular Greenspan in that era but now we're at risk of of throwing it out
claims.claim: Central bank inflation-fighting credibility, hard won under Volcker and Greenspan, is being squandered by cutting with inflation above target; because inflation embedded in the 1970s was so hard to wring out, this complacency is a very big risk.
claims.indicator: Fed cuts with inflation above target; inflation expectations
claims.direction: higher inflation risk premium; long yields up
claims.conditions: policy easing while inflation is above target and sticky
claims.testable: partly - inflation expectations and term premium after cuts above target
